lead: A datum is the reference surface and origin that gives coordinates meaning. Latitude, longitude and height are numbers until you say which surface they are measured from. A datum names the ellipsoid, how it sits on the earth, and the zero for heights. Surveyors, map makers and GNSS users rely on datums to combine measurements taken on different days and by different instruments. Without a datum, a coordinate is just a pair of numbers; with one, it points to a place on the ground.
prereq: You need: principles and classification of surveying; plane and geodetic for why earth curvature matters, and scales, maps and topographic sheets for how map positions are shown.

blocks.text: The geoid is the equipotential surface of earth's gravity field that best fits mean sea level, continued under the continents. Mean sea level is the average sea surface height recorded by tide gauges over a long period; it is not a flat plane. The geoid is lumpy because mass inside the earth is uneven: mountains, ocean trenches and dense rock pull the surface up or down by tens of metres.

An ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical surface made by rotating an ellipse about its short axis. It is fixed by two numbers: the semi-major axis a (equatorial radius) and the flattening f. The ellipsoid is simple enough for formulas, so survey computations use it instead of the geoid.

A datum pairs an ellipsoid with a position and orientation on the earth. A horizontal datum fixes latitude and longitude; a vertical datum fixes heights. WGS84 is a global datum used by GNSS. The older Indian datum, built on the Everest ellipsoid with its origin at Kalianpur, is a local example; the newer open series topographic maps of India are on WGS84. A datum is not a coordinate system; it is the surface that a coordinate system refers to.

Orthometric height H is the height of a point above the geoid, measured along the plumb line (the local vertical). It is the height that water levels and construction work use. A benchmark is a permanent mark, often a brass plate on a wall or pillar, whose reduced level (height above the vertical datum) is known from levelling. In India the benchmarks of the national levelling network carry reduced levels above mean sea level, and the spot heights on topographic sheets use the same vertical datum. How a level is carried from a benchmark, booked and reduced is taught with levelling.

GNSS receivers give ellipsoidal height h, measured above the ellipsoid. The geoid is not the ellipsoid, so the two heights differ by the geoid undulation N: the height of the geoid above the ellipsoid at that point.

blocks.where: H is orthometric height in metres; h is ellipsoidal height in metres; N is geoid undulation in metres, positive when the geoid lies above the ellipsoid.

blocks.text: If N is negative, the geoid lies below the ellipsoid and H is larger than h. A level survey and a GNSS survey at the same point will not agree until this correction is applied.

Geographic coordinates give a point by latitude φ, longitude λ (angle east or west of the prime meridian, which is 0° longitude) and a height. Latitude φ is the angle, measured at the point, between the normal to the ellipsoid and the equatorial plane, positive north; this is geodetic latitude, the latitude a map or GNSS receiver reports on that datum. Latitude and longitude need a horizontal datum; height needs a vertical datum. A point at 13.08° N, 80.27° E is a geographic coordinate, not a distance on the ground.

Projected coordinates flatten the ellipsoid onto a map plane using a map projection. The Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) system divides the earth into 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide, and gives easting and northing in metres. Easting is measured from the zone's central meridian with a false easting of 500 000 m added, so a point on the central meridian has easting 500 000 m, points to the west have less, points to the east have more, and every easting in the zone stays positive. Northing is measured from the equator, with a false northing of 10 000 000 m added in the southern hemisphere so northings stay positive there. UTM coordinates must state the zone and its hemisphere letter, for example 44N (zone 44, northern hemisphere), which is not the same thing as latitude 44° N. The mathematics of projections is taught with map projections in GIS. To find the zone of a longitude λ east, take zone = whole part of (λ + 180)/6, plus 1; its central meridian is 6 × zone − 183 degrees.

Cartesian coordinates use three perpendicular axes. Earth-centred, earth-fixed (ECEF) coordinates X, Y, Z have their origin at the earth's centre; the Z axis points near the north pole. GNSS computes in ECEF and then converts to latitude, longitude and height. When two sources use different datums, a datum transformation converts coordinates from the first datum to the second before they are mixed. Without that step, a shift of many metres can appear.

examples.question: A GNSS receiver on a survey pillar records ellipsoidal height h = 52.3 m. A geoid model gives the geoid undulation there as N = −82.0 m. (a) Find the orthometric height H. (b) A second point is reported as 13.08° N, 80.27° E on WGS84. Name the type of coordinates, find its UTM zone and central meridian, and say whether its easting is more or less than 500 000 m.
steps: Write the height relation: H = h − N.

Substitute: H = 52.3 − (−82.0). Subtracting a negative adds, so H = 52.3 + 82.0 = 134.3 m. The geoid lies 82.0 m below the ellipsoid here, so the point is higher above the geoid than above the ellipsoid.
(b) Latitude and longitude on a stated datum are geographic coordinates.
UTM zone = whole part of (80.27 + 180)/6, plus 1 = whole part of 43.38, plus 1 = 44. Central meridian = 6 × 44 − 183 = 81° E.
The point is 81 − 80.27 = 0.73° west of the central meridian, so its easting is less than the false easting: below 500 000 m (it is still positive).
examples.answer: H = 134.3 m. The second point is in geographic coordinates; it lies in UTM zone 44N, central meridian 81° E, and its easting is less than 500 000 m because it is west of that meridian.

traps: Sign of N: use H = h − N, never H = h + N. With N = −82.0 m and h = 52.3 m the wrong formula gives H = −29.7 m, a point below mean sea level, while the correct one gives H = 134.3 m. A negative N increases H.
Ellipsoidal height h and orthometric height H are not the same. h comes from GNSS; H is the height above the geoid.
Latitude and longitude need a horizontal datum; a height needs a vertical datum. A coordinate pair alone does not fix a height.
UTM easting and northing are meaningless without the zone and hemisphere.
When mixing coordinates from two datums, transform first. Do not average raw coordinates from WGS84 and a local datum.

quiz.a: The equipotential surface of earth's gravity field that best fits mean sea level, continued under the land.
A permanent mark with a known reduced level above the vertical datum, used as a starting point for levelling.

quiz.q: Why does a datum include an ellipsoid?
quiz.a: The ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical surface that formulas can use for coordinates and distances; the real geoid is too irregular for simple calculation.

quiz.q: A point has ellipsoidal height h = 100.0 m and geoid undulation N = −20.0 m. Find the orthometric height H.
A point is given as 13.08° N, 80.27° E. What type of coordinate is this?
quiz.a: Geographic coordinates, given by latitude and longitude.

quiz.q: If the geoid undulation N at a point is negative, how does the orthometric height H compare with the ellipsoidal height h?
quiz.a: H is larger than h. Because H = h − N and N is negative, H = h + |N|.

quiz.q: Why can a GNSS height differ from a levelled height at the same point by tens of metres?
quiz.a: GNSS gives ellipsoidal height h above the ellipsoid. Levelling gives orthometric height H above the geoid. The difference is the geoid undulation N, which can be tens of metres.

quiz.q: State the difference between a horizontal datum and a vertical datum.
quiz.a: A horizontal datum fixes the reference for latitude and longitude. A vertical datum fixes the zero surface for heights.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern GNSS augmentations broadcast corrections that include geoid models, so a receiver can output orthometric height directly. National geoid models are computed from gravity measurements and satellite data. In India, survey organisations maintain benchmark networks and geoid models for levelling and mapping. GIS software stores datum definitions with each layer, and reprojection is a routine step. Search for 'geoid model', 'datum transformation' and 'UTM zone' to go further.
